items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: A shape with finite volume but infinite surface area
items.claim: Rotate y = 1/x for x at least 1 around the x-axis. You get a 'horn' extending to infinity. Its volume is exactly pi (finite). Its surface area is infinite. You could fill it with paint, but never paint its interior.
items.prompt: How can volume be finite if surface area isn't?

options.text: The horn cannot be constructed in reality
Volume integrates 1/x squared (which is summable), while surface integrates 1/x (which is not); the integrals are independent, and one can converge while the other diverges
Surface and volume are always proportional in finite shapes

items.reveal:
Volume: V = pi * integral from 1 to infinity of (1/x) squared dx = pi * [-1/x] from 1 to infinity = pi.

Surface area: A = 2 * pi * integral from 1 to infinity of (1/x) * sqrt(1 + 1/x to the fourth) dx, which is greater than 2 * pi * integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x = infinity.

Intuition: volume scales as the square of the radius, surface as the radius. As you stretch toward infinity, the cross-sectional radius decreases as 1/x — the square (volume per unit length) decreases as 1/x squared (summable), but the radius itself (surface per unit length) decreases as 1/x (the harmonic series, divergent).

The 'paint paradox': filling the horn with pi cubic units of paint coats the interior — even though the surface 'should' need infinite paint to cover. The resolution: a paint film of any finite thickness doesn't fit at the horn's far reaches, where the radius is arbitrarily small.
items.why: Geometric intuition equates surface area and volume scaling. They're separate integrals; convergence of one doesn't imply convergence of the other.

items.title: A 1-in-300-million lottery ticket is almost always a bad investment
items.claim: Mega Millions: ~302 million possible combinations. A ticket costs $2. Jackpot of $600 million sounds like positive expected value (EV = 600M/302M = $2 — break even). But after taxes, lump sum discount, and ticket-splitting, real EV is well below $2.
items.prompt: How do you compute expected value correctly?

options.text: Sum over all outcomes of (probability * value). For a fair calculation, include ALL outcomes (not just the jackpot), tax adjustments, and the fact that big jackpots often have multiple winners who split the prize
Expected value is just the prize size

items.reveal:
Naive EV calculation for a lottery:
- Prize: $600M.
- Win probability: 1 / 302,000,000.
- EV from jackpot only: $600M / 302M ≈ $1.99.
- Ticket cost: $2.
- Naive net: -$0.01.

Real adjustments:
- Federal tax (~37% top bracket) plus state tax (variable, say 5%): take-home ~$330M instead of $600M.
- Lump sum vs annuity: lump sum is ~60% of advertised jackpot. Pre-tax lump sum: ~$360M. Post-tax: ~$200M.
- Jackpot splitting: when jackpots get large, more people play. Probability of multiple winners rises. Expected share is less than full jackpot.
- Other prizes: smaller wins (matching some numbers) contribute roughly $0.30 of EV per ticket. Better, but not enough.

Realistic EV: usually $0.50 - $1.00 per $2 ticket. Lottery is a regressive tax on the mathematically uninformed.

Linearity of expectation: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], even if X and Y aren't independent. A surprisingly powerful tool. The St. Petersburg paradox (already covered) is an exception where naive EV is infinite but psychological/practical value is finite.

Kelly criterion: optimal bet sizing when you have an edge. Even with positive EV, betting too much can lead to ruin. Bet fraction equals edge / odds. Most gamblers overbet, even when statistically lucky.

Applications:
- Insurance: companies sell policies with positive EV (for them); buyers accept negative EV in exchange for risk reduction.
- Investment decisions: long-run wealth is dominated by GEOMETRIC mean returns (Kelly).
- Game theory: mixed-strategy equilibria depend on equalising opponents' expected payoffs.
items.why: Expected value seems intuitive. Real computations require including hidden costs, taxes, and the structure of outcomes. The lottery survives because most players don't actually compute the math correctly — and because the entertainment value is real.
